cultivar: Fuding Dabai, Fuding Dahao, Zhenghe Dabai and Cai Cha
processing: Mature shoots of a small bud with three or four leaves and stem, withered for two to three days and dried at low temperature; no rolling or firing. Much of it is then steamed, pressed into cakes or bricks and slowly re-dried.
harvest_season: Late spring (late April to May) after the finer grades have been picked, and a large autumn harvest in September and October; the leaf is deliberately mature.
appearance_dry: Large, loose, mixed leaves in green, olive, brown and reddish tones with stems and the odd small bud; aged cakes turn brown-amber.
appearance_liquor: Gold to amber when fresh, deepening to orange-red with age.
appearance_wet: Big, soft, mature leaves and stems in olive to brown.
taste_profile: Mellow and sweet with hay, dried dates, honey and a woody, faintly herbal note; thick, smooth and very low in bitterness, deepening to jujube and a medicinal sweetness with age.

brewing.notes: Boiling water in a gaiwan or pot. Pry cakes into chunks rather than shredding them. Older Shou Mei is best simmered: a few grams in a litre, boiled gently for five minutes.

vintage_note: Sold overwhelmingly by year as pressed cakes (typically 300–357 g) and bricks, with young cakes of 1–3 years cheap and mid-aged 5–10 years the sweet spot; 'lao bai cha' cakes older than ten years are rare and often mislabelled. Fresh loose Shou Mei of the current spring or autumn is also sold cheaply. It is the white tea bought to age at home.
description:
Shou Mei, 'longevity eyebrow', is the big-leaf, low-grade white tea that has become the most interesting white tea to buy, because it is the one that gets pressed into cakes and aged. It is picked late, a small bud with three or four mature leaves and stem, after the Silver Needle and Mudan grades have been taken, and again in autumn, from the same northern Fujian bushes.

It is withered for two or three days and dried, like all white tea, and then most of it is steamed, pressed into 300–357 g cakes or bricks and dried again. The mature leaf is high in sugars and low in the tender compounds that make Mudan floral, so the tea starts mellow and sweet and gets rounder every year as the slow oxidation in the cake does its work.

Young, it tastes of hay, dried dates, honey and a little wood, thick and smooth and almost impossible to make bitter; after five or more years it turns to jujube, a warm herbal-medicinal sweetness and a deeper amber colour. Brew it with boiling water in a gaiwan or pot, breaking the cake into chunks rather than crumbs, and it runs seven steeps; older cakes are even better simmered for a few minutes on the stove, the way Fujian families drink it in winter.

Buying is all about the year. Cakes of one to three years are cheap and pleasant; five to ten years is the sweet spot for flavour and still affordable; anything claimed older than ten years should be approached with doubt, because pressing white tea only became widespread in the late 2000s and the supply of genuinely old cakes is tiny. Look for a cake that smells of dates and honey, not mustiness, and an amber rather than black liquor. Fresh loose Shou Mei of the current spring or autumn is sold too, and is a fine cheap daily tea.

Buy a few cakes of a young Shou Mei you like, store them dry and away from smells, and taste one every year: it is the cheapest way to learn how tea ages.
